Every part inspected

Only the hard cases leave the building.

Two vision-language models, fine-tuned on one HP ZGX Nano (NVIDIA GB10), inspect every part on the line. A person in the cloud looks only when a wrong automatic call would cost more than their time.

Open with the promise: "Every part inspected on the line. Only the hard cases leave the building." We built a working visual-inspection system that runs entirely on the HP ZGX Nano: two vision-language models we fine-tuned on the device itself, plus a cost rule that decides when a person in the cloud should look. Everything you'll see runs live on the Nano on this desk.
The brief

Local & Hybrid AI: inference on the ZGX Nano,
the cloud only when it is justified.

Event rule

The problem

A QC supervisor has about one second per part:
ship it, scrap it, or check it again.

It is launch week for a new product. There are hundreds of photos of good parts, a handful of defects, and designs the company will not upload to a vendor’s cloud yet.

of defects caught by human inspectors: the industry average (Sandia, 2015)
0%
of good parts rejected by inspectors in the same Sandia study
0 / 4,000
parts actually inspected under AQL 2.5 sampling; the rest ship unchecked
Oct 0 ’25
Amazon Lookout for Vision was discontinued. Cloud-only QC ties the line to one vendor

Our user: the line supervisor at a manufacturer launching a new product, who needs 100% inspection without the product’s images leaving the plant.

Meet our user: a QC line supervisor with about a second per part. Today they rely on people, who catch roughly 80–85% of defects and, in one Sandia study, rejected over a third of good parts. Or on AQL sampling, where most parts are never looked at. Cloud AI services exist, but Amazon Lookout for Vision was shut down in October 2025, and for a new product the images are the design. Press the arrow once more to reveal the user statement.
Why not just call a cloud vision API?

Four walls between the line and the cloud

🔒

Data residency

A new product’s photos are its design. Uploading every frame to a vendor is an IP leak waiting to happen.

⏱

Latency

A WAN round trip plus a queue on someone else’s GPU eats a one-second-per-part budget.

📡

Connectivity

When the plant’s internet drops, the line cannot stop. Inspection has to work offline.

💸

Per-call cost

At 60 parts/min for 16 h, a cloud vision LLM would cost about $89 / day per line (30M tokens, 66k calls).

So: decide on the edge, and use the cloud for the one thing it is good at: a person’s judgement on the rare hard case.

Why not a cloud API? Four reasons. Data residency: the images are the product's design. Latency: a round trip plus a remote queue doesn't fit a one-second budget. Connectivity: the line can't stop when the WAN drops. Cost: at GPT-4o-equivalent pricing, 60 parts a minute for two shifts is about $89 a day per line, from our real token counts. Reveal: decide on the edge, and use the cloud only for a person's judgement.
Existing solutions

How visual QC is done today, and where it breaks

ApproachHow it worksWeakness for a new product line
Human inspectionPeople look at every part, or at a sample~80–85% defect catch rate; tired eyes; up to a third of good parts rejected
AQL sampling (ISO 2859-1)Inspect a random sample per lotMost parts never inspected; a passing lot can still ship defects
Rule-based machine visionHand-tuned templates and thresholdsA vision engineer per product; brittle to new defects and lighting
Cloud AI inspectionUpload images to a vendorImages leave the plant; depends on the WAN and on one vendor
Anomaly detection (e.g. Anomalib)A score per image, on the edgeA score, not a decision: no defect name, no explanation, no action, no human loop
NanoInspectTwo fine-tuned local LLMs + a cost rule + the SOPInspects every part, names the defect and where it is, acts on the line, and asks a person only when it pays
A quick scan of the alternatives. People are inconsistent; sampling misses most parts; rule-based vision needs an engineer per product; cloud AI leaks the images; open-source anomaly detection gives a score, not a decision. We combine the best of each.
Our solution

A three-person inspection team, two of them on the Nano

Tier 1 · cheap LLM

Qwen2.5-VL-7B + our LoRA checks every part in ~2 s

Tier 2 · expensive LLM

Qwen3.8-27B + our LoRA compares doubtful parts with a known-good reference

Tier 3 · a person, in the cloud

Sees only a crop, and only when a review is cheaper than the risk

This is the operator app running on the Nano. Anyone can upload a photo, take a picture with a phone, or run three demo decisions. Behind it is a three-tier team: a cheap 7B vision-language model on every part, an expensive 27B model for doubtful parts, and a person in the cloud for the rare case where a review is cheaper than the risk of a wrong call.
Use case

Launch week at Plant-SJ, Line 3

1

Photograph

A few hundred good parts and a few dozen real defects, on the line’s own camera

2

Fine-tune on the Nano

LoRA adapters train on the device: 28 min (7B), 2 h 14 min (27B)

3

Inspect every part

~85% decided by tier 1 in ~2 s; rejects get a machine instruction

4

Escalate the hard 5.6%

Only a 5 KB crop reaches a reviewer, queued through outages

5

Reviewer labels return to the Nano as new training data

The use case as a flow. Day one: photograph good parts and some real defects. Fine-tune on the Nano; no image goes anywhere. Then every part is inspected, most by tier 1 in about two seconds. The hard 5–6% go to a reviewer as a 5 KB crop. And the green loop: reviewer labels come back to the Nano as training data for the next fine-tune, so it keeps improving. Below is the live overview dashboard, in full: parts inspected, share decided on the edge, image data kept on-site, the decision cascade per tier, and GPU telemetry.

Here's the flow, animated at our measured rates. Every part hits tier 1. If its probability of a defect is low, it's accepted on the spot; that's about 85% of parts. Unsure parts, plus a 5% random audit, go to tier 2, which sees the part next to a known-good reference. Only when tier 2 can't settle it, because the models disagree or tier 2 can't answer, and the cost rule says a review is worth it, does a person see a crop. That's 5.6% of parts.

Explicit · defensible · measurable

When does a part go to the cloud? Try it.

escalate ⇔ min( P(defect) × $escaped_defect , P(good) × $scrapped_part ) > $human_review
Evidence bucket → P(defect), by Bayes’ rule from held-out error rates
Accept
–
expected cost P × escape
Reject
–
expected cost (1−P) × scrap
Human review
–
reviewer’s time

Fitted on one half of the held-out images and reported on the other. The costs belong to the plant (quality manager and SOP), not to us, and are editable in the app.

This is our answer to "explicit, defensible, measurable". Each part lands in an evidence bucket: both agree it's good, both agree it's defective, they disagree, and so on. From held-out error rates and the line's defect rate, Bayes' rule gives the probability of a defect, and we pick the cheapest action. Click "tier 1 flags, tier 2 says good": P is 3%, accepting risks $1.57, rejecting $1.94, a review costs $0.50, so it goes to a person. Click "both see a defect": P is 80%, rejecting costs $0.40, so it's rejected on the edge. Drag the escape cost up to show the rule move.

No added wait for explanations

The untrained 27B writes the operator’s sentence in parallel with the fine-tuned 27B’s verdict on the same server.

The first novelty is that we optimised every layer, not just the model. Decision: we minimise expected cost per part, and in capacity mode the tier-1 threshold is set from tier 2's measured throughput. That takes us from $500 to $230 per thousand parts. Model: LoRA trains under half a percent of the weights, and the probability of a defect comes for free from the verdict token's log-probabilities: one pass, no second call. Serving: vLLM batching gives 16× throughput, plus prefix caching and an FP8 KV cache. Hardware: the difference map runs on the Grace CPU so the GPU memory goes to the LLMs. The result: 74% less GPU energy than running the 27B on every part.
What’s new · 2

Hybrid AI, turned around: the cloud gets people, not pixels

Typical hybrid AI
Edge camerafull imagesCloud model decidesper callResult back
✕ images leave the plant✕ $ per call✕ stops without WAN✕ vendor’s model, not yours
NanoInspect hybrid
Two LLMs decide on the Nanodisagreements only · 5 KB cropA person reviewslabelNano retrains
✓ full images stay✓ $0 per model call✓ works offline (queued)✓ you own the fine-tuned model

Rule fixed before training

Keep the 27B fine-tune only if the whole pipeline gets cheaper. It did ($415.24 → $411.91), so it stays. The baseline is tagged in git.

Actions come from the SOP

The LLM picks from the plant’s ISO 9001 SOP. It can’t invent a disposition, and every message is schema-validated.

Knows what it doesn’t know

Unreadable or unfamiliar frames go straight to a person: 0 of 9 broken inputs were accepted.

The second novelty is how we use the cloud. Typical hybrid AI sends images to a bigger cloud model: images leave, you pay per call, and it stops without the WAN. We turn that around. Both models are on the Nano; only disagreements leave, as a 5 KB crop, and they go to a person, not a model. The person's label comes back and the Nano retrains, so you own the model. Three more firsts: a keep-or-revert rule fixed before training, actions constrained to the plant's SOP, and a system that sends unfamiliar input to a person rather than guessing.

We stress-tested the device, not just the model. 15 minutes with both LLMs saturated: 2,671 plus 180 inferences, zero errors, max 70 °C, no throttling. 13.7 joules per tier-1 check. Throughput scales from 0.5 to 8.3 parts per second. We pulled the network (zero outbound connections, inspections kept running) and fed it broken frames and a dead model server. Nothing broken was ever accepted.

Both models were fine-tuned on the Nano with LoRA. The big weight matrix stays frozen; only two thin adapter matrices learn, under half a percent of the weights. Training data is real defect photos only: half of every defect type, with the other half held out for testing. Tier 1 went from catching 21% of defects zero-shot to 84%. For tier 2, the keep rule was fixed before training, and it passed.

The LLMs’ edge over ResNet: ResNet gives a score. Our models also say what the defect is (78%) and where it is (81%), in words an operator can act on, with 3× fewer false alarms.

Results, on 1,096 images no model trained on. The fine-tuned 27B catches 94% of defects, more than the ResNet classifier, while flagging only 4.7% of good parts versus ResNet's 14.8%: three times fewer false alarms. Unlike ResNet, it names the defect type 78% of the time and the location 81% of the time. Fine-tuning improved every tier-2 metric, including a 24-point jump in naming the defect.

Live on the Nano · three real parts, three outcomes

Accept, reject, human review

Every result shows the part, the difference heatmap vs. 40 good parts, where the LLM says the defect is, and the known-good reference. Operators can chat with tier 2 about any part.

Switch to the live app here if time allows; otherwise click through the three tabs. Accept: a good bottle; tier 1 is confident, accepted in under two seconds, no big model, no person. Reject: a broken rim; tier 1 flags it, tier 2 confirms "the rim of the bottle opening is severely chipped", rejecting is cheaper than a review, and the line gets a divert instruction. Review: contamination; tier 1 flags it but tier 2 sees nothing. They disagree, so a reviewer gets the crop. Disagreement is exactly what people are for.
From verdict to action

Every reject becomes an instruction the line can execute

{
  "schema": "nanoinspect.disposition/v1",
  "product": "tile", "station": "Tile pressing + glazing",
  "sop": { "sop_id": "QA-SOP-NI-001", "version": "1.0" },
  "disposition": "reject",
  "line_command": { "target": "diverter", "action": "divert_to_reject_bin" },
  "nonconformance": {
    "ncr_id": "NCR-20260925-00001",
    "defect_type": "crack", "severity": "critical", "location": "center",
    "probable_cause": "kiln thermal shock",
    "process_check": "Check kiln cooling curve",
    "rework_allowed": false
  },
  "containment": { "stop_line_if_repeats": 3, "window_parts": 20,
                   "notify": ["line supervisor", "quality engineer"] }
}

The SOP decides the action, not the LLM

ISO 9001 §8.7, “control of nonconforming outputs”. The plant’s procedure (config/sop.json) lists the dispositions, causes and checks for all 73 defect types. The model may only choose from it.

Validated and auditable

Every message is checked against a JSON Schema and carries the SOP id and version. Repeated defects trigger stop_line automatically.

A decision alone doesn't help a line. Every reject becomes schema-validated JSON for the PLC or MES: divert to the reject bin, a nonconformance report, the probable cause and a process check. Those come from the plant's own SOP, per ISO 9001 clause 8.7; the LLM can only pick causes the SOP lists. If a defect repeats three times in 20 parts, it stops the line.

This is why a company would trust it. Watch the live flow: every frame lands in the Nano and stays there; the counter of kept megabytes keeps growing. Only rarely, when a part is escalated, does a tiny crop travel through the gate to a person in the cloud, and a green label comes back. The bytes-kept percentage stays above 99%; in our live session it was 99.7%. Below: what stays (images, weights, training data, adapters), what leaves (only a 5 KB crop, with an API key, queued through outages), and what is never in the cloud (no AI, no full images, no weights).
For the IT / security team

How an organisation deploys it with zero leakage

1 · Set up once, then air-gap

Weights download once (setup.sh). Then run offline and block all egress at the firewall except the review host.

2 · Own the cloud tier

The review console is a Docker image: run it in your VPC or on-prem. Set a private NANOINSPECT_CLOUD_KEY and put TLS in front.

3 · Minimise what leaves

Crops only, and only on escalation. Tune the crop size, or keep escalations on-site entirely for a fully local line.

4 · Harden the box

Full-disk encryption, SSH keys only, services on localhost (as shipped), HTTPS for the app, and zrt’s auth + TLS proxy in front of the models.

5 · Audit everything

Every decision logs the model, the SOP id and version, and schema-validated JSON, for ISO 9001 records.

6 · Keep the IP

Adapters are trained on the device from your photos and stay yours: no vendor model learns your product.

Built into the prototype: localhost binding, optional HTTPS, crop-only escalation, API-key auth, no cloud AI, offline operation, on-device training, SOP audit trail. Recommended at deployment: egress firewall, TLS for the cloud tier, disk encryption, a retention policy for the cloud database, and HP Z Runtime’s TLS proxy (already on).

For the IT and security team, a six-step playbook. Download weights once, then air-gap the box, allowing only the review host. Run the cloud tier, a Docker image, in your own VPC. Minimise what leaves: crops only, or none for a fully local line. Harden the box: disk encryption, SSH keys, HTTPS, and HP Z Runtime's auth and TLS proxy in front of the models. Audit every decision against the SOP version. And keep the IP. Reveal the footer: we're honest about what's built versus recommended.

Each tile is a real held-out part being scanned, and the red box is the true defect. Electronics, pharma (where GMP data can't leave the site), automotive, packaging, textiles, building materials, food and consumer goods. Onboarding is the same everywhere: photograph, fine-tune on the Nano (under an hour for tier 1), run. Honest trade-offs · what’s next

What we’d do with another month

Trade-offs we measured

• Training needs the 27B’s full-precision weights; we serve it in FP8: same accuracy, 1.8× faster (0.84 vs 0.46 parts/s)
• Capacity mode tops out at about 50 parts/min per Nano
• MVTec AD is a benchmark, not a live line

Roadmap

• Try NVFP4 for the fine-tuned 27B (FP8 already gives 1.8×)
• Closed loop: nightly retraining from reviewer labels, with the same keep-or-revert rule
• OPC UA / MQTT to real PLCs; drift alerts
• Pilot with a real camera fixture; a fleet sharing a defect library, not images

We're upfront about trade-offs. The fine-tuned 27B runs in full precision, so it's half as fast as the quantised build; quantising it is next. Capacity mode tops out around 50 parts a minute per Nano. MVTec is a benchmark, so a real-line pilot comes next. The roadmap: nightly retraining from reviewer labels, serving through HP Z Runtime, real PLC integration and drift alerts.
